## TL;DR

The original auth-less failure was expected at the API boundary, but the UI’s 401 handling was incomplete. It could display empty-state actions after access was denied, and mutation failures could leave sensitive drafts and confirmation context mounted. The Secrets view now transitions into one explicit sign-in-required state, clears stale UI and cached page data, and suppresses actions that cannot succeed until access is restored. Regression tests cover cold and warm 401s, all relevant mutation paths, and the signed-in server handlers.

`REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed. The remote build and changed-path test suite passed, as did the rendered contrast audit and UI smoke test. Local format, lint, build, contrast, and UI smoke checks also passed.

## Work and rationale

Review round 2 identified a state-lifecycle problem beyond the initial empty page. A 401 from key removal could leave its confirmation dialog mounted after the rest of the page had been cleared. The selected environment was then empty, making the dialog’s context confusing; a later reload could also allow an old confirmation to act against refreshed data. Saving a key had a related failure mode: the typed key/value, add or edit form, and prior success banner could remain mounted after the page switched to an authentication error.

The view’s shared 401 handler now clears the state that belongs to the inaccessible page: cached environments and snapshot metadata, selection, add/edit and removal dialogs, open menus, drafts, create form contents, and stale status messages. It also invalidates the page-data cache so that a later authenticated visit does not reuse data captured under the previous session. The page presents the fixed sign-in guidance and hides the empty-project prompt and its creation actions while unauthorized. A failed mutation therefore cannot leave an actionable dialog or a typed secret behind the sign-in state.

The handler remains shared with the other Secrets page errors, while mutation handlers route `ApiError` instances through it when the status is 401. This avoids rendering a server response such as “Authentication required” in one path and the user-facing sign-in guidance in another. The existing 401 handling for the editor-launch path likewise uses stable UI copy rather than reflecting raw server text.

The UI regression tests use the actual 401 body (“Authentication required”). They assert that a cold unauthorized page does not show a create-environment call to action, that a warm page removes previously loaded environment and key metadata on expiration, and that removal confirmation and save/create/edit forms and draft values are cleared. The edit case seeds a success message before triggering the later 401, ensuring stale status copy is cleared too. The tests use only fake secret values and assert that values are not included in rendered unauthorized content.

For authenticated behavior, I added a route-handler integration test that creates a valid admin session and invokes the real project-environment listing and key-metadata handlers. It verifies successful responses and expected environment/key metadata, while confirming the dotenv source value is not returned by the metadata endpoint. That documents the server-side security model and provides an authenticated API path test without depending on an interactive browser session.

The unauthorized page state also has a registered preview fixture that renders the sign-in guidance without loading project secrets. This provides deterministic UI fixture coverage. The existing declared screenshot capture continues to use the populated fixture, so it should not be interpreted as proof of a live signed-in request or as a capture of the unauthorized state.

## Approaches tried

I first traced the UI’s existing `safeError` path and the mutation handlers named by review rather than treating the initial screenshot as evidence of an authenticated regression. The review findings reproduced as separate but related state-lifecycle cases: a cold 401, an expired session after loading data, a key-removal confirmation, and create/save form state. Consolidating cleanup in the common unauthorized handler keeps those cases aligned and avoids future handlers inventing partial cleanup behavior.

I considered whether client-only tests could establish signed-in access. They cannot prove the real route’s authorization behavior, so I added a server route test using the repository’s auth-session fixture and actual handlers. It checks the route response shape and output omission of the source value. I did not attempt a live browser login in this run; the route test is the authenticated verification evidence, not a claim of an end-to-end browser session.

## Challenges and blockers

The scoped check ran remotely and took several minutes because it selected a broad changed-path test set. An initial remote session stopped returning output before a final status was available, so I restarted the exact required check and followed the new run through its final result. The second run completed successfully. No code or test failure blocked the work.

A real interactive login and browser inspection were not performed. The authenticated server test covers the API authorization path and the UI tests cover its handling of success and 401 responses, but it is not a live browser round trip. Also, the deterministic unauthorized fixture is registered in code but the existing task screenshot declaration is still the populated fixture; no screenshot capture of the unauthorized UI is claimed here.

## Key learnings

A page-level authentication error needs to be treated as a state transition, not just an error string. Clearing the data model alone is insufficient when dialogs, form drafts, typed secret values, and success messages live in independent reactive state. Each access-denied response should converge on one cleanup policy so the page cannot retain actions or contextual metadata from the prior session.

The task’s original 401 was expected because the endpoint requires sign-in. That fact did not make the observed UX acceptable: empty-state creation prompts and leftover mutation UI could imply actions that cannot work or retain stale context. Pairing the fixed sign-in state with explicit UI cleanup handles the actual product defect while preserving the API’s authenticated access model.

Finally, evidence should be labeled by what it proves. A populated fixture demonstrates rendering only; a valid-session route test demonstrates authenticated handler behavior; and a live browser login would demonstrate the complete session-to-page flow. This run has the first two kinds of evidence, not the third.
